title: Data Engineering, Machine Learning and Model Evaluation
summary: Building MealSenseAI's food classifier: two public datasets merged into one 320-class taxonomy, audited for leakage and conflicting labels, and used to fine-tune EfficientNet-B0 on a self-hosted GPU.
meta: Python · PyTorch · EfficientNet-B0 · CUDA · Docker · FastAPI · PostgreSQL
Ubuntu Linux · NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM)

paragraphs: MealSenseAI estimates the nutrition of everyday meals from a photograph, with a focus on Singaporean and Southeast Asian dishes that general food datasets cover poorly. It combines computer vision, transfer learning, nutrition-database mapping and small language models (SLMs).
This work produced its classifier: one model over a unified food taxonomy, built from two public datasets whose labels were harmonised and whose quality was checked before any accuracy was measured.
Two labelled image datasets pair international coverage with Singapore-specific dishes.
Combined: 310,861 images and 334 class entries, harmonised into 320 classes — broader coverage than either source alone, especially for food eaten in Singapore.
Every image was checked for integrity and duplication.

blocks.label: Why it matters.
blocks.text: A duplicate that lands in both training and test leaks the answer and inflates accuracy; duplicates with conflicting labels teach the model contradictions. Both have to be found before a score means anything.

paragraphs: The two datasets overlap and name foods differently. Their 334 class entries — 10 of them exact matches once names were normalised — were consolidated into an approved taxonomy of 320 classes, used for both training and inference.

items: RGB standardisation and resizing to a consistent input resolution
Pixel normalisation compatible with the pretrained network
Augmentation — rotation, flips, crops, zoom, brightness and contrast — on the training partition only, so validation and test stay independent

paragraphs: The classifier uses transfer learning on EfficientNet-B0, an architecture that balances accuracy against compute. Its pretrained visual features were kept and the classification layers adapted to the unified taxonomy, rather than training a network from scratch.

paragraphs: GPU execution under CUDA was validated, and checkpoints from both experiments were retained for evaluation and integration.
The framework uses standard multiclass measures, alongside the cost of running the model.

head: Measure
What it shows
rows: Reliability of predictions, coverage of true classes, and their balance
Which foods are mistaken for each other

paragraphs: Each run records its dataset version and partitions, architecture and checkpoint, configuration, epoch-level metrics, evaluation outputs, runtime and GPU performance, with timestamps — so any result can be reproduced and traced.

blocks.label: Status.
blocks.text: The dataset audit, both training experiments, GPU validation and checkpoints are documented. Final accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and confusion-matrix values are being verified against the saved experiment outputs and are not published until they are.

paragraphs: The classifier is one stage of a modular inference pipeline. The person confirms or corrects each prediction before it counts.

Keeping inference separate from application services lets detection, classification or nutrition analysis improve without redesigning the app. The aim is diabetes-aware insight — carbohydrate awareness and meal composition — as estimates, not medical advice.

items: Consolidated two datasets — 310,861 images — into a 320-class taxonomy
Audited integrity and duplication, exposing potential leakage and label conflicts
Built a transfer-learning workflow on EfficientNet-B0, with baseline and fine-tuning stages and retained checkpoints
Validated GPU-accelerated training on a self-hosted CUDA workstation with consumer hardware
Designed a modular architecture linking computer vision, nutrition data and SLM explanations

paragraphs: Good machine learning is more than choosing and training a model: dataset quality, consistent labels, reproducible experiments, efficient compute and integration into the product matter as much.

Image-based nutrition estimation has real limits — mixed dishes, irregular portions and foods that look alike. Next: better multi-food instance segmentation, portion estimation and confidence calibration, and validation against independently labelled images.
